title: Symmetry-Aware Bayesian Optimization via Max Kernels
one_liner: When you are optimizing something with hidden symmetries, align similarities within symmetry orbits to learn faster.
lead: Bayesian Optimization is a method for finding the best setting of something when testing it is expensive (like tuning a robot's arm, or tuning wireless network antennas). When you know the objective has symmetries (for instance, a robot arm getting the same score after a 90-degree rotation as it did before), you can exploit those to reduce wasted experiments. This paper shows that the best way to do this is to measure similarity not by averaging across all symmetries, but by finding the single best alignment between two options within their symmetry orbits.

paras: Imagine optimizing a wireless network where you want to place antennas to cover a town. Rotating the entire layout by 90 degrees gives you the same coverage. So your optimizer will test the original layout, then test a rotated version, then a mirrored version, wasting evaluations on things it should already know are equivalent.

A naive first attempt: just average over all rotated versions of each option when comparing them. But this dilutes the signal because the Bayesian Optimizer uses a similarity function (a kernel — a rule for how alike two points are) to learn which regions are promising; if a good placement scores 95 at angle 0 and 40 at angle 90, averaging gives 67.5—the same as a mediocre placement scoring 67.5 everywhere. The optimizer cannot distinguish them and wastes evaluations exploring both.

callout.html: Instead of averaging a score across all symmetries, find the single best alignment between two options' symmetry versions.

paras: The paper replaces the kernel — the function that measures similarity between two candidate solutions — with one that respects the best alignment within symmetry orbits, then projects it to obey mathematical rules.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: orbit alignment quality
hidden.name: Best alignment within symmetry orbits
paras: An orbit is the set of all versions of a solution you can get by applying symmetries. For two solutions, the max kernel measures their similarity by the best alignment pair between their orbits. If one antenna layout rotated 45 degrees matches another rotated 90 degrees very closely, the max kernel captures that high similarity directly.

The paper estimates this by computing the similarity between every pair of rotated versions, then taking the maximum. This keeps the signal sharp: if one placement is genuinely better for most rotations, its high scores do not get diluted by averaging.

heat.caption: Darker means sharper signal. Best alignment (max) captures true similarity; averaging dilutes it. Validity means the math works.

reads.html: When two things can be rotated or flipped in multiple ways, pick the rotation pair that makes them most similar. That similarity tells you whether they are really the same thing or different things.

The max kernel measures the best-aligned similarity between two solutions across all symmetry pairs. It is invariant by construction but not positive semidefinite on its own, so we project it via the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse to restore mathematical validity.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: signal preservation via alignment
paras: Bayesian Optimization uses a Gaussian process to guess the shape of the objective. The kernel (similarity measure) teaches the process what closeness means. If you average similarities across all symmetries, you lose the sharp differences: a good placement that scores well under rotation 0 and poorly under rotation 90 averages to medium, indistinguishable from a mediocre placement that scores medium everywhere. The max kernel avoids this by saying: two options are as similar as their best-aligning pair. So a genuinely good placement stays sharply distinct from a mediocre one.

The catch: maximizing violates a mathematical rule called positive semidefiniteness, which the Gaussian process needs to make valid probability statements. The paper fixes this by projecting the max kernel onto the space of valid kernels using the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse. This is not fudging; it is finding the closest valid kernel to the max kernel. On the finite set of evaluated points, the projection preserves the max kernel exactly (no loss of information). Off that set, it smoothly interpolates. This means you get the sharp signal-preservation of max with the mathematical guarantees of a proper Gaussian process.

stages.s: Project via Moore-Penrose to restore math validity

math.words: The kernel is computed by projecting the max-aligned kernel onto the valid mathematical space. On the points you have already evaluated, it exactly matches the max kernel. On new points, it interpolates smoothly.
math.equation:
k_max(x, x') = max_{g, g' in G} k_base(gx, g'x')    [step 1: raw max]
k_+(D)(x, x') = phi(x)^T phi(x')  where  phi(x) = K_+^(1/2) k_max(D, x)    [step 2: projected form]
symbols: the base kernel, which measures similarity directly
the symmetry group (the set of all symmetries that preserve the objective)
the max kernel: pick the best alignment
the design set: all points evaluated so far
the kernel matrix of the max kernel on D; the pseudo-inverse K_+^(-1) undoes it
the feature representation; the product phi(x)^T phi(x') equals k_+(D)
the projected kernel: mathematically valid and sharp-signal-preserving

worked.title: A tiny worked example: 1D antenna placement with mirror symmetry
lines: Antennas at positions x=1 and x'=1 (same place): both can be mirrored at x=-1. Original positions score 0.8 agreement. Mirrored positions also score 0.8. Max alignment = 0.8.
Antennas at x=1 and x'=2 (different places): original pair scores 0.5, but when we mirror x'=2 to -2, it aligns poorly with mirrored x=-1 (score 0.2). Best pair is original: max=0.5.
Antennas at x=1 and x'=3 (far apart): no rotation helps; max=0.1. After projection to valid kernel space, the score stays roughly 0.1 (not much to project).
Because antenna problems often have many weak placements and few good ones, max kernels keep the signal sharp. Averaging would muddy all three examples toward 0.4.

math.note: The projection step ensures the Gaussian process can compute valid uncertainties, while keeping max-kernel's sharp signal on the points you have tested.

items.b: Symmetry group is wrong or incomplete.
items.html: If you tell the optimizer that rotations are a symmetry but the true objective breaks under some rotations, the method will miss those breaks and misguide the search.

items.b: Base kernel is too weak for the objective.
items.html: Max alignment works only if the base kernel (the similarity function you provide) actually captures relevant closeness in your problem. A bad base kernel makes max alignment useless.
If your symmetry group is huge (e.g., all possible permutations of 100 antenna positions), computing max over all pairs becomes prohibitively expensive.

Provide an honest symmetry group, a base kernel that fits your domain, and a manageable orbit size. Max-kernel projection will outperform averaging because it preserves sharp differences in quality across symmetries, letting the Gaussian process confidently guide the next evaluations toward good regions instead of averaging away the signal.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small Bayesian Optimization problem with obvious symmetry. For instance, minimize a 2D function that is invariant under 90-degree rotations (like distance from the center, or a radially symmetric gaussian). Set up three kernels: the base kernel alone, an average-over-orbits kernel, and the max-kernel-projected kernel. Run each optimizer for the same budget of evaluations (say, 50 function calls).
demo.metric_eq: regret = (best possible score) - (best score found by the optimizer after each evaluation)
demo.closing: Plot cumulative regret over iterations. The max-kernel-projected method should converge faster to good regions because its kernel preserves sharp signals, letting the Gaussian process steer confidently toward symmetry equivalents of already-tested good placements.
